chunks: Preemphasis: why and how. The question: What is preemphasis? Why is it used? How can it be implemented?
A long trace or cable weakens the fast-changing parts of a signal more than the slow parts, so sharp edges arrive rounded and bits smear into each other.
Preemphasis fixes this at the sender. The transmitter deliberately exaggerates the fast parts, by about as much as the cable will take away.
The signal that arrives is then close to the one you wanted.
Imagine steering a heavy, sluggish car. To change lanes quickly, you yank the wheel hard at first and then ease it back once the car starts moving.
If you turned only to the final angle, the car would drift over slowly. Preemphasis does the same to a bit stream.
The first bit after a change is driven at full strength to overcome the sluggish line. Repeated bits are driven softer.
The sender can't exceed its maximum output voltage, so in practice repeated bits are turned down.
The red curve is the channel falling to about minus 8 decibels at 5 gigahertz. The blue dashed curve is the 2-tap FFE, rising by 6 decibels.
Their sum (green) is within about 2 decibels of flat out to Nyquist, instead of 8 decibels down.
Because the FFE boost is a cosine of frequency and the channel loss is smooth, a 2-tap filter approximates the inverse only roughly, so real links use 3 taps and a receiver CTLE/DFE as well.
Channel: everything the signal travels through, such as the trace, connectors and cable ("TL loss and distortion sources").
Transition: a bit that differs from the one before it, like a 0 followed by a 1.
Inter-symbol interference (ISI): the tail of one bit spilling into later bits and confusing the receiver. De-emphasis: driving repeated bits lower than transition bits.
It is the same trick as preemphasis, measured from a different reference. Boost: how much stronger the fast parts are than the slow parts, in decibels (dB).
6 decibels means twice the height.
Suppose the sender mixes 75% of the current bit with 25% of the opposite of the previous bit. A bit after a change comes out at full height, 1. 0. A repeated bit comes out at 0.
75-0. 25 equals 0. 5 . Fast switching is therefore 2 times, or 6 decibels, stronger than a long run of the same bit.
A channel that loses about 6 decibels on fast switching then evens it out. That is the whole idea.
"Preemphasis boosts the high-frequency part of the transmitted signal to cancel the low-pass response of a lossy channel, so the received signal is flat and ISI is small.
In the time domain it overshoots the first bit after a transition, or equivalently de-emphasizes repeated bits.
It's usually a short FIR filter in the driver, like y[n] equals (1-a)x[n]-a x[n-1] , which boosts Nyquist by 1 over (1-2a) . It can also be a passive RC network.
The cost is lower low-frequency swing, more high-frequency EMI and crosstalk, and coefficients that need tuning."
